message.content:
I don’t have access to live sensor feeds, so I can’t tell you the exact AQI for Los Angeles at this very moment.  However, here’s what you can do to get the current air‑quality information:

| Source | How to check | Typical data you’ll see |
|--------|--------------|------------------------|
| **AirNow** (U.S. EPA) | Visit <https://www.airnow.gov/> and enter “Los Angeles, CA” | Current AQI (0–500), pollutant breakdown (PM₂.₅, O₃, NO₂, etc.) |
| **AQICN** (World Air Quality Index) | Go to <https://aqicn.org/city/los-angeles/> | Real‑time AQI, forecast for next 24 h, historical trends |
| **Weather apps** (e.g., Weather.com, AccuWeather, Apple Weather) | Search “Los Angeles” | AQI displayed alongside temperature, humidity, etc. |
| **Local news** (e.g., KABC, KNBC) | Check their weather/air‑quality segments | Often report “moderate” or “unhealthy” levels during peak smog season |

### Typical Los Angeles air‑quality pattern

- **Spring (March–May)** – Often the worst period.  Ozone peaks after midday; PM₂.₅ can rise from 10–20 µg/m³ to 30–40 µg/m³.  AQI frequently falls into the **“Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups”** (101–150) or even **“Unhealthy”** (151–200) range.
- **Summer (June–August)** – Ozone remains high, especially on sunny days.  PM₂.₅ usually stays lower than in spring, but can still reach **“Moderate”** (51–100) or **“Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups”** levels.
- **Fall (September–November)** – Ozone tends to drop, but wildfire smoke can push PM₂.₅ into **“Unhealthy”** or **“Very Unhealthy”** ranges if fires are active in the region.
- **Winter (December–February)** – Generally better, but temperature inversions can trap pollutants, leading to occasional **“Moderate”** or **“Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups”** readings.

If you’re planning outdoor activities or have respiratory concerns, it’s best to check a real‑time source right before you head out.  Let me know if you’d like a quick guide on interpreting AQI values or tips for minimizing exposure during high‑pollution days!
